turns.reply: Welcome! Everything electrical, from your phone to a kettle, works because charge flows round a circuit, and today we start with the basic idea of electric current: the rate of flow of electric charge, measured in amperes (A). So if current is about how fast charge flows, what unit do we measure current in?

Not quite: coulombs measure the amount of charge, not the current. Current is how fast that charge flows, a bit like litres per second for water in a pipe, and its unit is the ampere (A). So which unit do we use for current?

Yes — the ampere (A) is the unit of current. Charge is what we measure in coulombs (C), and 1 coulomb is the charge that flows past a point in 1 second when the current is 1 ampere (A). So if the current is 1 ampere (A), how much charge passes a point every second?

Yes — 1 coulomb passes every second when the current is 1 ampere (A). Now for the energy side: potential difference (p.d.) tells you how much energy is transferred for each coulomb of charge that flows between two points, and it is measured in volts (V). So what unit do we measure potential difference in?
recap: Current is the rate of flow of electric charge.
Current is measured in amperes (A).
Charge itself is measured in coulombs (C), so don't mix them up.
A current of 1 ampere means 1 coulomb passes a point each second.

turns.reply: No worries, let me say it more simply. Potential difference is the "energy push" the charge gets: it tells you how much energy each coulomb of charge carries between two points, and we measure it in volts (V). So what is the unit of potential difference?

Yes — volts (V) is the unit of potential difference. Now for resistance: it is the opposition to the flow of current, and it is measured in ohms (Ω). So if the resistance in a circuit goes up, what happens to the current for the same potential difference?
recap: Potential difference is the energy push the charge gets.
It tells you the energy transferred per coulomb between two points.
The unit of potential difference is the volt (V).
One ampere means one coulomb of charge passing every second.

turns.reply: Not quite: more resistance means more opposition, so less current flows. Picture a narrow pipe: the narrower it is, the less water gets through. So if the resistance in a circuit goes up, what happens to the current for the same potential difference?
Yes, current goes down when resistance goes up. The unit of resistance is the ohm (Ω), and 1 ohm is 1 volt per ampere. So what is the unit of resistance, written as its symbol?
Yes, that's the right idea. The symbol is the Greek letter omega, written Ω, and it stands for the ohm. So what is the symbol for ohms?

Yes, Ω is right, the symbol for the ohm. Next, an I-V characteristic is a graph that shows how the current through a component changes as the potential difference across it changes. Current (I) goes on the y-axis. So which quantity goes on the x-axis?
recap: Resistance is how much a circuit opposes the flow of current.
More resistance means less current for the same potential difference.
Think of a narrow pipe letting less water through.
Resistance is measured in ohms, written with the symbol Ω.

turns.reply: Yes, potential difference (V) goes on the x-axis. An ohmic conductor, such as a fixed resistor at constant temperature, gives a straight line through the origin, so doubling V doubles I. If V doubles from 2 V to 4 V and the current was 1 A, what will the current be?

Let me say that more simply. For an ohmic conductor, the graph is a straight line, and if V doubles, I doubles too. So if V goes from 2 V to 4 V and the current at 2 V was 1 A, what is the current at 4 V?

turns.reply: That's fine, you can come back to this lesson any time. The answer was 2 A, because doubling V doubles I. Next, a diode only lets current flow in one direction, the forward direction, and it has a very high resistance in the reverse direction. So which direction has the very high resistance?

Yes, the reverse direction is right, because that's where the diode has very high resistance. In the required practical, you test a filament lamp, a diode and a resistor, and you use a variable resistor (rheostat), a resistor whose resistance can be changed, to vary the current. So what do we change on the variable resistor to change the current?
recap: An I-V graph plots current (y-axis) against potential difference (x-axis).
An ohmic conductor gives a straight line through the origin.
Double the potential difference and the current doubles too, like 1 A becoming 2 A.
A diode lets current through one way, with very high resistance in reverse.

turns.reply: Fair enough, I'll keep it short. A variable resistor is a resistor you can adjust, and changing its resistance changes the current in the circuit. So if you turn it to make the resistance bigger, what happens to the current?

Yes, a bigger resistance means a smaller current, that's right. To measure the current you use an ammeter, an instrument that is connected in series with the component, meaning in the same loop with it. So how is the ammeter connected to the component?

Yes, in series is right, because the ammeter sits in the same loop as the component. A voltmeter measures potential difference (p.d.) and is connected differently: in parallel with the component, meaning across it on its own side loop. So how is the voltmeter connected to the component?

Yes — in parallel, across the component, is right. That brings us to the end of this lesson. You answered questions on electric current, potential difference, resistance, I-V characteristics and the required practical, though only briefly, since we kept things short. Well done for sticking with it.
recap: Test a filament lamp, a diode and a resistor in this practical.
A variable resistor changes the resistance, which changes the current.
Bigger resistance means smaller current.
Ammeter goes in series; voltmeter goes in parallel, across the component.
